blind_target.title: Do defaults save lives?
blind_target.evidence_quote: In two well-powered samples (N = 1920), we conducted a close replication of the default effect in Johnson and Goldstein (2003) and in Johnson, Bellman, and Lohse (2002).
blind_target.outcome_quote: We successfully replicated Johnson and Goldstein (2003).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Overall verdict confirms this target despite smaller effects; both samples contributed to Part 1.

blind_target.evidence_quote: We based our extension on Van Dalen and Henkens (2014) who found that organ donation rates were higher when the option was temporary and would have to be renewed than when the default option was to donate.
blind_target.outcome_quote: In the first extension, we predicted that people would be more inclined to become donors when consent to organ donation is temporary. We found no evidence that consent varied between the temporary and permanent conditions.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Extension 1 explicitly retests this cited temporal-choice finding in Sample 1. The supplied cache lacks its reference entry; title and DOI cannot be copied.
